complications.name: Diabetic Retinopathy
complications.source_text: Diabetic retinopathy is a highly specific neurovascular complication of diabetes, with prevalence strongly related to both the duration of diabetes and the level of chronic.

complications.name: Diabetic Macular Edema
complications.source_text: At any point along this spectrum, the retina vasculature can leak fluid (and exudates) leading to diabetic macular edema (DME).

complications.name: Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy
complications.source_text: In response to ischemia, neovascularization can occur; this is proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR).

complications.name: Diabetic Peripheral Neuropathy
complications.source_text: Individuals who have had type 1 diabetes for 5 years and all individuals with type 2 diabetes should be assessed annually for DPN using medical history and simple clinical tests (63).

complications.name: Loss of Protective Sensation
complications.source_text: The involvement of large fibers may cause balance issues (including falls), numbness, and loss of protective sensation (LOPS).

complications.name: Diabetic Foot Ulcer
complications.source_text: If not recognized and if preventive foot care is not implemented, people with diabetes are at risk for injuries as well as diabetic foot ulcers (DFUs) and amputations.

complications.name: Cardiovascular Autonomic Neuropathy
complications.source_text: CAN is associated with mortality independent of other cardiovascular risk factors (68,69).

complications.name: Gastroparesis
complications.source_text: Gastroparesis should be suspected in individuals with erratic glycemic management or with upper gastrointestinal symptoms without another identified cause.

complications.name: Charcot Foot
complications.source_text: Individuals considered at risk should understand the implications of foot deformities, LOPS, and PAD; the proper care of the foot, including nail and skin care; and the importance of daily foot inspections.

complications.name: Peripheral Artery Disease
complications.source_text: Management of people with diabetes and PAD requires not only careful assessment but also both holistic and interventional approaches.

complications.name: Nephropathy
complications.source_text: Retinopathy, nephropathy (particularly individuals on dialysis or posttransplant)

screening_tests.name: Dilated Eye Examination
screening_tests.source_text: Adults with type 1 diabetes should have an initial dilated and comprehensive eye examination by an ophthalmologist or optometrist 5 years after the onset of diabetes.
screening_tests.frequency: 5 years after onset for T1D, at diagnosis for T2D, annually thereafter if no retinopathy

screening_tests.name: 10-g Monofilament Testing
screening_tests.source_text: All people with diabetes should have annual 10-g monofilament testing to identify feet at risk for ulceration and amputation.
screening_tests.indication: Identify feet at risk for ulceration and amputation

screening_tests.name: Neurological Assessment
screening_tests.source_text: Assessment for distal symmetric polyneuropathy should include a careful history and assessment of either temperature or pinprick sensation (small-fiber function) and vibration sensation using a 128-Hz tuning fork (large-fiber function).

screening_tests.name: Autonomic Neuropathy Screening
screening_tests.source_text: Symptoms and signs of autonomic neuropathy should be assessed in people with diabetes starting at diagnosis of type 2 diabetes and 5 years after the diagnosis of type 1 diabetes, and at least annually thereafter
screening_tests.test_name: Assessment for symptoms of autonomic neuropathy

screening_tests.name: Foot Examination
screening_tests.source_text: Perform a comprehensive foot evaluation at least annually to identify risk factors for ulcers and amputations.
screening_tests.indication: Identify risk factors for ulcers and amputations

screening_tests.name: Vascular Assessment
screening_tests.source_text: The examination should include inspection of the skin, assessment of foot deformities, neurological assessment (10-g monofilament testing or Ipswich touch test with at least one additional assessment: pinprick, temperature, or vibration), and vascular assessment, including pulses in the legs and feet.
screening_tests.test_name: Vascular assessment (pulses in legs and feet)

screening_tests.name: Retinal Photography
screening_tests.source_text: Programs that use retinal photography with remote reading or the use of U.S. Food and Drug Administration–approved artificial intelligence algorithms to improve access to diabetic retinopathy screening are appropriate screening strategies for diabetic retinopathy.

therapeutic_agents.name: Anti-VEGF Agents
therapeutic_agents.source_text: Intravitreous injections of anti–vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) are a reasonable alternative to traditional panretinal laser photocoagulation for some individuals with PDR and also reduce the risk of vision loss in these individuals.
therapeutic_agents.when_to_use: Proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR), Diabetic Macular Edema (DME)

therapeutic_agents.name: Panretinal Laser Photocoagulation
therapeutic_agents.source_text: Panretinal laser photocoagulation therapy is indicated to reduce the risk of vision loss in individuals with high-risk PDR and, in some cases, severe nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy.
therapeutic_agents.when_to_use: High-risk PDR, severe nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy

therapeutic_agents.name: Gabapentinoids
therapeutic_agents.source_text: Gabapentinoids, serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors, tricyclic antidepressants, and sodium channel blockers are recommended as initial pharmacologic treatments for neuropathic pain in diabetes A.

therapeutic_agents.name: Serotonin-Norepinephrine Reuptake Inhibitors
therapeutic_agents.source_text: Gabapentinoids, serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors, tricyclic antidepressants, and sodium channel blockers are recommended as initial pharmacologic treatments for neuropathic pain in diabetes A.

therapeutic_agents.name: Tricyclic Antidepressants
therapeutic_agents.source_text: Gabapentinoids, serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors, tricyclic antidepressants, and sodium channel blockers are recommended as initial pharmacologic treatments for neuropathic pain in diabetes A.

therapeutic_agents.name: Sodium Channel Blockers
therapeutic_agents.source_text: Gabapentinoids, serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors, tricyclic antidepressants, and sodium channel blockers are recommended as initial pharmacologic treatments for neuropathic pain in diabetes A.

therapeutic_agents.name: Metformin
therapeutic_agents.source_text: Gastrointestinal neuropathies are a diagnosis of exclusion (including consideration of gastrointestinal adverse effects due to medications such as metformin and/or GLP-1–based therapy).

therapeutic_agents.name: GLP-1 Receptor Agonists
therapeutic_agents.source_text: Gastrointestinal neuropathies are a diagnosis of exclusion (including consideration of gastrointestinal adverse effects due to medications such as metformin and/or GLP-1–based therapy).

therapeutic_agents.name: Aspirin
therapeutic_agents.source_text: The presence of retinopathy is not a contraindication to aspirin therapy for cardioprotection, as aspirin does not increase the risk of retinal hemorrhage (54).

therapeutic_agents.name: Fenofibrate
therapeutic_agents.source_text: In individuals with dyslipidemia, retinopathy progression may be slowed by the addition of fenofibrate, particularly with early diabetic retinopathy at baseline.

risk_factors.name: Chronic Hyperglycemia
risk_factors.source_text: Chronic hyperglycemia is the best-established concomitant risk factor associated with microvascular complications (e.g., diabetic retinopathy and neuropathy).

risk_factors.name: Duration of Diabetes
risk_factors.source_text: Diabetic retinopathy is a highly specific neurovascular complication of diabetes, with prevalence strongly related to both the duration of diabetes and the level of chronic.

risk_factors.name: Hypertension
risk_factors.source_text: In addition to diabetes duration, factors that increase the risk of, or are associated with, retinopathy include chronic hyperglycemia (6,7), nephropathy (8), hypertension (9), and dyslipidemia (10–12).

risk_factors.name: Dyslipidemia
risk_factors.source_text: In addition to diabetes duration, factors that increase the risk of, or are associated with, retinopathy include chronic hyperglycemia (6,7), nephropathy (8), hypertension (9), and dyslipidemia (10–12).

risk_factors.name: Nephropathy
risk_factors.source_text: In addition to diabetes duration, factors that increase the risk of, or are associated with, retinopathy include chronic hyperglycemia (6,7), nephropathy (8), hypertension (9), and dyslipidemia (10–12).

risk_factors.name: Obesity
risk_factors.source_text: Obesity is consistently associated with neuropathy in cross-sectional and longitudinal studies.

risk_factors.name: Smoking
risk_factors.source_text: Factors that are associated with the at-risk foot include the following: ... Smoking

referral_criteria.name: Referral for Diabetic Retinopathy
referral_criteria.source_text: If diabetic retinopathy is evident on screening, prompt referral to an ophthalmologist is recommended.
referral_criteria.criteria: Evidence of diabetic retinopathy on screening

referral_criteria.name: Referral for Sight-Threatening Retinopathy
referral_criteria.source_text: More frequent examinations by the ophthalmologist will be required if retinopathy is progressing or risk factors such as not meeting glycemic goals, advanced retinopathy, or DME are present.
referral_criteria.criteria: Progressing retinopathy, not meeting glycemic goals, advanced retinopathy, DME

referral_criteria.name: Referral for Moderate or Worse Nonproliferative Diabetic Retinopathy
referral_criteria.source_text: 12.9 Promptly refer individuals with any level of diabetic macular edema, moderate or worse nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy (a precursor of proliferative diabetic retinopathy [PDR]), or any PDR to an ophthalmologist who is knowledgeable and experienced in the management of diabetic retinopathy.
referral_criteria.criteria: Any level of diabetic macular edema, moderate or worse nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy, or any PDR

referral_criteria.name: Referral for Atypical Neuropathy
referral_criteria.source_text: Electrophysiological testing, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan of the spine (66), or referral to a neurologist is rarely needed, except in situations where the clinical features are atypical (acute or subacute presentation, non–length dependent, asymmetric, and/or motor involvement) or the diagnosis is unclear.
referral_criteria.criteria: Atypical clinical features of neuropathy or unclear diagnosis

referral_criteria.name: Referral for High-Risk Feet
referral_criteria.source_text: An interprofessional approach facilitated by a podiatrist in conjunction with other appropriate team members is recommended for individuals with foot ulcers and high-risk feet (e.g., those on dialysis, those with Charcot foot, those with a history of prior ulcers or amputation, and those with PAD).
referral_criteria.criteria: Foot ulcers, high-risk feet (on dialysis, Charcot foot, history of prior ulcers/amputation, PAD)

referral_criteria.name: Urgent Referral for Foot Complications
referral_criteria.source_text: Individuals with any open ulceration or unexplained swelling, erythema, or increased skin temperature should be referred urgently to a foot care specialist or interprofessional team.
referral_criteria.criteria: Open ulceration, unexplained swelling, erythema, or increased skin temperature
